title: NAT, ICE, and the ALG problem
summary: Why embedded addresses break, and what rport, STUN, TURN, ICE, SIP ALGs, and media latching each actually do.

lessons.title: Embedded addresses and NAT
lessons.summary: SIP and SDP embed IP addresses. NAT rewrites the packet header and leaves those embedded addresses behind.
objectives: Find addresses in Via, Contact, and SDP c=
Explain why a packet-header NAT does not fix those fields
Treat a private connection address as non-routable from the public peer

illustration.title: Two places an address can sit
illustration.caption: NAT sees the outer header. SIP and SDP also name addresses in the payload.

layers.name: Via and Contact
layers.detail: Where responses and later requests go

layers.name: SDP c= and m=
layers.detail: Where RTP is supposed to go

sections.h: The address is inside the message
paragraphs: SIP puts addresses in Via and Contact, and SDP puts an address in c= and a port in m=. Those fields are what the peer uses for the next signaling hop and for RTP.

A NAT changes the source address on the IP packet and does not understand the SIP body, so the embedded address can still name a host the public peer cannot reach. The call then rings, or even answers, while media has nowhere routable to go.

sections.h: What a correct synthetic offer looks like
paragraphs: In this lab the offer uses the documentation address 203.0.113.10 in c=, which is a public documentation address from RFC 5737 and is the address the example intends the carrier to use. Contact uses that same documentation address so signaling and the description agree.

When c= instead carries a private address, that address is non-routable on the public Internet. The carrier at 192.0.2.40 cannot send RTP there. Fix the address the public peer will see, or use a mechanism from a later lesson, and do not expect the NAT to have edited c=.

lessons.title: rport and symmetric responses
lessons.summary: RFC 3581 adds rport so the response is sent to the source address and port the request came from.
objectives: Add rport on Via when you need symmetric response routing
Read received and rport on the response Via
Keep rport separate from RTP NAT traversal

illustration.title: Where the response goes
illustration.caption: The server answers the source it observed. rport does not rewrite SDP.

paragraphs: RFC 3581 defines the rport Via parameter for symmetric response routing. The client puts rport on Via, and the server sends the response to the source IP address and source port of the request instead of trusting only the host and port written in Via.

The server adds received with the source address it saw and fills rport with the source port it saw. In this lab the Via host is 203.0.113.10 port 5060 and the observed source port is 49160, so the response is aimed at port 49160.

rport fixes the return path for SIP responses. It does not change c=, and it does not move RTP. A call can complete signaling through rport and still have one-way or no audio because the media address is a separate field.
Use rport together with a media solution from the later lessons when the RTP address is also wrong. Do not treat a filled-in rport parameter as evidence that SDP was rewritten.

lessons.title: STUN server-reflexive addresses
lessons.summary: STUN, RFC 8489, lets a client learn the address a server sees. It obsoletes RFC 5389.
objectives: State that RFC 8489 obsoletes RFC 5389 and where status is decided
Describe a Binding request as a way to learn a server-reflexive address
Keep STUN separate from a SIP registrar

illustration.title: Learn the address the server sees
illustration.caption: The reflexive address is what STUN observed. It is not a SIP Contact by itself.

paragraphs: STUN is RFC 8489, which obsoletes RFC 5389. The RFC Editor status banner is the authority for that status. A Binding request asks a STUN server to tell the client the source address and port the server observed.
That observed address is the server-reflexive address, and the response attribute used for it is XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS. STUN is not SIP, and a STUN server is not a SIP registrar.

sections.h: What you do with the result
paragraphs: ICE, in a later lesson, uses this address as a candidate of type srflx. STUN by itself does not rewrite a SIP INVITE and does not allocate a relay.

If both peers are behind NATs that refuse unsolicited inbound UDP, a reflexive address may still be unreachable. That limit is why TURN exists, and it is not a reason to put a private address in c= and hope.

lessons.title: TURN relays
lessons.summary: TURN, RFC 8656, allocates a relay when host and server-reflexive paths fail. It obsoletes RFC 5766.
objectives: State that RFC 8656 obsoletes RFC 5766 and where status is decided
Describe Allocate as the way a client gets a relayed address
Use the relay only as a media path, not as a SIP registrar

illustration.title: A relay when direct paths fail
illustration.caption: The relay address is allocated. It is candidate type relay in ICE.

paragraphs: TURN is RFC 8656, which obsoletes RFC 5766. The RFC Editor status banner is the authority for that status. The client sends Allocate, and the server reserves a relayed transport address that both sides can send media through.
Permissions control who may send to that relay. TURN is a media relay, not a SIP proxy and not a rewrite of Via. The relay address in this synthetic network is 198.51.100.30.

sections.h: When the relay is the path
paragraphs: Use TURN when host and server-reflexive candidates cannot carry the media. The remote peer sends RTP to the relayed address, and the TURN server forwards it to the client.
ICE is the negotiation that chooses the relay instead of guessing. Putting the relay address into c= by hand, with no Allocate and no candidate line, is not a TURN session.

lessons.title: ICE candidate types
lessons.summary: ICE is RFC 8445, which obsoletes RFC 5245. Candidates are host, srflx, prflx, and relay.
objectives: Name the four candidate types
State that RFC 8445 obsoletes RFC 5245 and where status is decided
Let connectivity checks choose the pair

illustration.title: Four candidate types
illustration.caption: prflx is discovered during checks. It is not usually in the first offer.
rows: The address a STUN server observed
An address learned from a connectivity check

paragraphs: ICE is RFC 8445, which obsoletes RFC 5245. The RFC Editor status banner is the authority for that status. Each side gathers candidates and puts them in SDP, then both sides run connectivity checks and nominate a pair that actually passes packets.

The candidate types are host, srflx, prflx, and relay, and each one names a different place the media address came from. A host candidate is a local interface, srflx is the server-reflexive address from STUN in RFC 8489, and relay is the TURN address from RFC 8656. A prflx, or peer-reflexive, candidate appears when a check arrives from an address that was not already in the list.

sections.h: Checks, not the order of the lines
paragraphs: A higher-priority candidate is not used until a check succeeds. ICE can nominate a relay even when a host candidate is listed first, if the host candidate cannot receive packets from the peer.
c= remains in the SDP for agents that do not do ICE, and ICE agents still follow the check result for media. Do not delete the candidate lines and keep only c= when you meant to run ICE.

sections.h: What the answer must still do
paragraphs: ICE rides inside offer/answer, so the answer still has the same number of m-lines in the same order, and a rejected stream is still port 0. Candidate lines add addresses for checks, and they do not replace that m-line rule.
An SBC that strips a=candidate and leaves a private c= line has removed the traversal information and kept the address that does not route. Pass the candidates or terminate ICE on the SBC on purpose.

lessons.title: The SIP ALG problem
lessons.summary: A SIP ALG rewrites SIP and SDP in transit and often corrupts the call. It cannot rewrite TLS.
objectives: Recognize an in-path rewrite of Via, Contact, or c=
Treat a broken Content-Length after a rewrite as corruption
Prefer TLS when you need the ALG to be unable to edit the body

illustration.title: UDP is visible, TLS is not
illustration.caption: The ALG is not an SBC you configured. It is an unexpected editor on the path.

sections.h: An editor you did not configure
paragraphs: A SIP ALG rewrites addresses inside SIP and SDP as the message crosses a NAT. The intent is to fix the embedded-address problem, and the usual result is a corrupted call, because the rewrite is partial or it leaves Content-Length stale.

Look for a Via or c= line that changed between two captures of the same request, and for a Content-Length that does not match the body, because those are the symptoms of an ALG edit. The fix is to disable the ALG on the access device.

sections.h: TLS is opaque to the ALG
paragraphs: The ALG cannot rewrite TLS, because the SIP headers and the SDP are inside the protected connection. A trunk that uses TLS, with a certificate checked under RFC 5922, does not get its c= line edited in flight.
Disabling the ALG and using TLS are the two practical responses. Do not add a second uncoordinated rewrite on an SBC to chase the damage, or you will have two editors and no original message.

lessons.title: Media latching on an SBC
lessons.summary: Many SBCs learn the remote RTP address from the first packet instead of trusting c=. That is deployment practice, and RFC 5853 is the requirements RFC.
objectives: Describe latching as learning RTP from the first packet
Cite RFC 5853 as requirements, not as an algorithm
Refuse to move the latch toward an unexpected source

illustration.title: c= versus the packet you saw
illustration.caption: Latching is something many SBCs do. RFC 5853 collects requirements. It is not an IETF algorithm.

paragraphs: Many SBCs learn the remote RTP address from the first packet instead of trusting c=. RFC 5853 is the requirements RFC for SBC deployments, and it is the right citation for why operators ask for this behavior.

That behavior is deployment practice rather than an IETF algorithm. You will not find a standards-track state machine that says the first packet wins. When you document a design, say what the SBC does and cite RFC 5853 as requirements.

sections.h: Trust the latch only after signaling
paragraphs: Latching exists because c= is often an address the SBC cannot send to, which is the embedded-address problem. The first RTP packet shows the address that actually got through the NAT.

Use latching only for a call whose signaling you already authenticated, and keep the latch on the peer side you expect. If the first packet comes from an unexpected source, treat that as a fault and do not move the media path. ICE, RFC 8445, remains the specified way to choose a candidate pair when both ends implement it.
